blocks.title: Introduction
blocks.content: It is a known fact that many standard (integer) linear programming formulations of relevant problems in optimization show a lot of symmetry. In this situation a standard branch-and-cut framework repeatedly enumerates symmetric solutions, and sometimes this renders such methods useless. To address these issues the last decade saw a number of approaches to devise algorithms specialized to symmetric optimization problems. blocks.title: Searching Integer Layers Efficiently
blocks.content:
[]{#sec:searching label="sec:searching"} The question remaining is how to test ILP-feasibility of a $c$-layer in an efficient way. Our key observation is that some optimal integral solution is close to the fixed space if the group of symmetries acts sufficiently transitive.

::: definition
Given a $c$-layer with center $z$, an integral point in the $c$-layer is a *core point* if it minimizes the distance to $z$.
:::

blocks.title: Finding All Symmetries
blocks.content:
[]{#sec:finding label="sec:finding"} For the algorithms presented it is never necessary to know the entire group of automorphisms of $\operatorname{LP}(A,b,c)$ or $\operatorname{ILP}(A,b,c)$. Generally, any subgroup will do, the larger the better. Yet here we would like to discuss the question of how to find automorphisms of integer linear programs. From the input data we will construct a labeled graph $\operatorname{G}(A,b,c)$ whose group of labeled automorphisms coincides with $\mathop{\mathrm{Sym}}(\operatorname{ILP}(A,b,c))$.

blocks.title: Wild Input
blocks.content: One way to produce symmetric input for (integer) linear optimization algorithms is by brute force: One can take any system $Ax\le b$ of linear inequalities and let the full group $\mathop{\mathrm{Sym}}(n)$ act. This way each original inequality may give up to $n!$ inequalities in the resulting *symmetrized* system. The symmetrized system of inequalities is $\mathop{\mathrm{Sym}}(n)$-invariant by construction.
